forces: Soprano solo, mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Lisa della Casa, soprano; Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg; live
intro: The Requiem begins with bassoons and basset horns winding around one another, before the choir takes up their prayer. Bruno Walter conducts this Salzburg performance, with Lisa della Casa singing the soprano psalm verse.

sections.label: Intro · Bassoons and basset horns
sections.mNote: Overlapping reed phrases above short, off-beat strings

sections.label: A · The choir takes up the prayer
sections.mNote: Basses, tenors, altos and sopranos enter in turn

sections.label: B · A soprano sings the psalm
sections.mNote: A wind link leads to the solo in B♭ major

sections.label: A′ · The basses begin again
sections.mNote: The prayer returns with a quicker accompanying vocal line

sections.label: Coda · The prayer rests on A
sections.mNote: Quiet voices hold the dominant under a fermata

cues.title: Low reeds, restless strings
cues.text: A bassoon begins; a basset horn answers before the phrase is over. The basset horn is a low member of the clarinet family. Beneath these long wind notes, the strings take short, uneven steps, with rests cutting into the beat.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 1–2, bars 1–7. Basset-horn description: Jan Swafford, https://www.bso.org/works/mozart-requiem. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP758680-PMLP2751-Mozart_Requiem%2C_K.626_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The choir builds upwards
cues.text: The basses begin the prayer for eternal rest. Tenors, altos and sopranos follow in turn, taking up the phrase heard first in the winds. Around them the violins make sharp, falling leaps, each pair of notes separated from the next by a rest.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 2, bars 8–12: successive choral entries and the paired violin figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mozart’s finished first movement
cues.text: Mozart dies in Vienna on 5 December 1791, leaving the Requiem unfinished. This opening movement is already fully scored. The completion used for the rest of Walter’s performance is Süssmayr’s.
cues.evidence: Jan Swafford, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/mozart-requiem. Leopold Nowak’s Neue Mozart-Ausgabe foreword describes the surviving score and its completion: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf

cues.title: One voice in B♭
cues.text: The choir falls silent. A brief wind link leads to the soprano’s psalm verse in B♭ major, with running violin lines around it. Mozart leaves the organ out beneath this solo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 3–4, bars 17–25: senza Org., the instrumental link and the soprano Te decet hymnus.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Count Walsegg copies the score
cues.text: Count Franz von Walsegg commissions the Requiem in memory of his wife. Before conducting it in December 1793, he copies out the score and heads it “Requiem composed by Count Walsegg”.
cues.evidence: Leopold Nowak, Neue Mozart-Ausgabe, Requiem, volume 2, foreword, p. IX, citing Anton Herzog’s account: Walsegg’s copy bears Requiem composto del Conte Walsegg; he conducts the memorial service on 14 December 1793. Translation here is our own. https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf

cues.title: Two pleas at once
cues.text: The basses bring back “Requiem aeternam”, while the altos thread a quicker line around them on “Dona eis” — grant them. The prayer for rest and the act of asking unfold together. Soon the sopranos take up the running line too.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 6–7, bars 34–43: the returning theme and the quicker dona eis line pass between the choral parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A held breath on A
cues.text: The last request for light grows quiet. Choir and orchestra settle on A major, the chord that points back towards D minor, and hold it under a fermata. The Kyrie’s D-minor fugue follows in the complete work.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 8, bars 46–48: piano, A-major dominant and fermata, followed by the Kyrie at Allegro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The wind phrase finds words
transitions.to: A · The choir takes up the prayer
transitions.how: Brass announce the choir, whose basses begin the D-minor prayer. Tenors, altos and sopranos follow with the opening wind phrase. The violins change from short off-beat notes to falling pairs, leaving a rest between each pair. The instrumental bass keeps its interrupted tread as the voices accumulate above it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 1–3, bars 7–14.

transitions.title: The organ falls silent
transitions.from: A · The choir takes up the prayer
transitions.to: B · A soprano sings the psalm
transitions.how: The first choral prayer subsides into B♭ major. A short phrase for basset horns and bassoons bridges the gap before the soprano psalm. The organ falls silent; cellos and running violin figures accompany the solo voice. The marking remains Adagio.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 3–4, bars 17–25, including senza Org. beneath the transition.

transitions.title: The basses recover the prayer
transitions.from: B · A soprano sings the psalm
transitions.how: After the psalm, a quiet wind link recalls the opening. The basses recover “Requiem aeternam” in D minor, and the altos add a quicker curling phrase on “Dona eis”. The violin leaps return around them. Two vocal ideas now travel through the choir together.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 6–7, bars 32–43: wind link and the two interwoven vocal ideas.

transitions.title: A major holds the door open
transitions.to: Coda · The prayer rests on A
transitions.how: The choir softens to piano for its last request for light. The bass settles on A, and the voices hold an A-major chord under a fermata. This dominant chord prepares the D-minor fugue of the following Kyrie.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 8, bars 46–48 and the opening of the Kyrie.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–8: the bassoon and basset-horn introduction, successive choral entries, soprano psalm and return of the opening prayer.

timeline.note: A bassoon begins above short string notes; the organ follows the bass line without adding chords.
Bassoons and basset horns overlap while both violin parts take up the off-beat pulse.
The choir enters from basses upwards; trumpet and timpani accents punctuate the prayer.
A quiet phrase for basset horns, bassoons and strings links the choral prayer to the soprano psalm; the organ rests.
The soprano sings above running violin and cello figures, with the organ silent.
The choir takes over the psalm; the strings continue their quick figures beneath it.
The opening prayer returns in the basses, with quicker phrases passing through the other voices and falling leaps in the violins.
Choir and strings soften towards the held A-major chord; trumpets and timpani support the close.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lisa della Casa (soprano), Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Mozart’s completed Introitus, within the traditional Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem; performing edition unidentified.
fields.note: The NMA distinguishes the Introitus, fully orchestrated by Mozart, from the incomplete later movements. The file contains this complete opening movement, stopping before the Kyrie. The traditional version is an identification from the repertory and score comparison, not an edition named by the upload. Walter’s precise instrumental alterations are unestablished.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
fields.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides

Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
